source.title: Doubly-Special Relativity: First Results and Key Open Problems

accepted.question_text: How should Doubly-Special Relativity describe macroscopic bodies? The paper treats Planck-scale deformations of the dispersion relation as acceptable for microscopic particles because presently observable particle energies are far below the observer-independent scale Ep, but notes that ordinary macroscopic bodies typically have total energies far above Ep. The open problem is to formulate a DSR description in which planets, soccer balls, and other macroscopic systems are not forced into phenomenologically unacceptable Planck-scale kinematics while preserving the DSR framework for microscopic particles.

evidence.quote: 7.1. How should one describe macroscopic bodies in DSR?

Planck-scale deformations of the dispersion relation are clearly admissable for microscopic particles, since we produce/observe these particles with energies that are much smaller than Ep and therefore the predicted new effects are small enough to comply with present experimental limits.

Instead macroscopic bodies typically have energies largely in excess of Ep, and the assumption of a Planck-scale deformation of the dispersion relation is in clear conflict with observations as ordinary as the motion of planets in the solar system and the game of soccer.

It has been clear from the beginning that the DSR framework automatically includes structures that may be useful in settling satisfactorily this issue, but a full satisfactory understanding/description is still missing.

accepted.question_text: What should count as a DSR observer, and how should observer-dependent measurements be modeled when the theory may require macroscopic observers using different kinds of probes? The paper suggests that Planck-scale deformation may not apply to the observer as a macroscopic system and that high-energy probes could alter perceived time dilation, length contraction, and related measurements. The unresolved problem is to give a genuine description of DSR observers and determine, in particular, whether the relation between rapidity and relative velocity remains the special-relativistic one or must itself be modified.

evidence.quote: 7.2. What is the DSR observer?

It appears likely that the theory will require the obsever to be a macroscopic system, to which the Planck-scale deformation does not apply. Since we lack a description of macroscopic bodies, we are also still lacking a genuine understanding of DSR obsevers.
For example, in a context probed with high-energy probes the observer might experience a different type of time dilatation and leangth contraction. But this has not yet been investigated.

At the merely technical level these issues concerning the DSR observer are relevant for establishing the relation between rapidity and relative velocity among observers. Is this relation modified? Or should we still adopt the special-relativistic relation between rapidity and relative velocity?

accepted.question_text: Which spacetime descriptions are compatible with the Doubly-Special Relativity framework? The robust results obtained so far concern only the energy-momentum sector, while the paper argues that introducing a second observer-independent scale may require a major revision of spacetime concepts, possibly even abandoning the absolute statement that two particles follow the same trajectory for all observers. The open problem is to identify a spacetime picture, possibly involving noncommutative geometry or only an approximate notion of spacetime, that is consistent with DSR kinematics and with the relation v = dE/dp if that relation is retained.

evidence.quote: 7.3. Which spacetimes are compatible with the DSR framework?
All robust results obtained so far in the DSR framework concern the energy-momentum sector. It is unclear which type of spacetime picture is required by the DSR framework.
What should we give up for the second observer-independent scale?

Perhaps this is taking us in the direction of considering spacetime as an approximate concept, only valid within a certain class of observations and with a certain level of approximation. Perhaps such a picture could be implemented through a description of spacetime in terms of noncommutative geometry.

accepted.question_text: Can a Doubly-Special Relativity theory explain the apparent Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin (GZK) cosmic-ray anomaly by producing a sufficiently large modification of the threshold for pion production of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays on cosmic microwave background photons? The paper notes that DSR generically changes thresholds, but specifically states that the known DSR1 and DSR2 constructions shift the GZK limit only very slightly. The unresolved problem is whether some other DSR theory can produce a significant change in the GZK limit while remaining compatible with the relativity principle.

evidence.quote: 7.4. Can DSR solve the GZK anomaly?

While DSR theories do generically predict anomalous thresholds (and therefore generically predict a different value of the GZK limit), as mentioned in DSR1 and DSR2 the change in the value of the GZK limit is very small, and could not be used to explain away the paradoxical ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray observations.
Even looking beyond DSR1 and DSR2 it appears hard to find a DSR theory which would significantly affect the GZK limit.

accepted.question_text: How should causality be understood in Doubly-Special Relativity theories, especially those in which photon speed increases with energy and arbitrarily high-energy particles would propagate superluminally relative to ordinary low-energy light? The paper argues that these features may have profound implications for causal structure, cosmology, and operational notions of time, including whether access to ultra-high-energy probes could make time approximately absolute for some observers. The open problem is to formulate a full DSR account of causality and its observational consequences.

evidence.quote: 7.5. What about causality?
In a significant portion of DSR theories, including DSR1, there appear to be also profound consequences for causality.
These theories predict that ultra-high-energy photons would travel faster than the low-energy photons which we ordinarily observe/study (for which it is well established that they travel at speed c).
But a full understanding of DSR causality is clearly a key objective of this research programme.

accepted.question_text: How should the DSR program be extended from inertial observers and deformed special relativity to noninertial observers and a corresponding modification of general relativity? The paper states that no robust results had yet been obtained and emphasizes that the Planck scale may need to play a double role, both through the gravitational coupling linked to G and through the structure of spacetime or energy-momentum space. The open problem is to build a consistent general-relativistic extension of DSR that reconciles these two roles of the Planck scale.

evidence.quote: 7.6. What about noninertial observers?

Of course, since the DSR research programme is considering a modification of Special Relativity, a natural next step to consider is the one in which an analogous modification is implemented at the level of General Relativity.
Nothing that can claim any robusteness has been obtained so far on this interesting point.

I believe that a key issue for such studies comes from the observation that we might be required to attribute to the Planck scale a double role: a role in the gravitational coupling (because of the relation between G and Ep) and a role in the structure of spacetime (energy-momentum space).
